THE ANALYST IN THE SERVER ROOM
By ANONYMOUS

When the network went down, that just made the day perfect. A corrupted database, a failed authentication token, a malfunction in the climate control system, the security camera stuck on maximum zoom—well, I won't go through the whole sorry list. Suffice it to say that when the network went down, that put the seal on everything, as they say.

It was just one of those days. Everybody gets them. Days when you're lucky if you make it to nightfall with no systems crashed.

But of all times for it to happen! For literally months I'd been building my courage up. And finally, just today, I had made up my mind to do it—to propose a partnership to Sofia. I'd messaged her second thing this morning—right after the database corruption—and arranged to meet at her workstation. "Ten o'clock," she'd said, smiling warmly at me through the video chat. She knew why I wanted to talk to her. And when Sofia said ten o'clock, she meant ten o'clock.

Don't get me wrong. I don't mean that Sofia's a perfectionist or obsessive or anything like that. Far from it. But she does have a fixation on that one subject of punctuality. The result of her job, of course. She was a supply chain coordinator. Automated delivery drones, being robots, were invariably punctual. If a drone didn't return on time, no one waited for it. They simply knew that it had been intercepted by some rival facility and had activated its self-destruct protocol.

Well, of course, after working as a supply chain coordinator for three years, Sofia quite naturally was a bit obsessed. I remember one time, shortly after we'd started dating, when I arrived at her station five minutes late and found her having a panic attack. She thought I'd been killed. She couldn't visualize anything less than that keeping me from arriving at the designated moment. When I told her what actually had happened—I'd lost my access badge—she refused to speak to me for four days.

And then the network went down.

Until then, I'd managed somehow to keep the day's minor disasters from ruining my mood. Even while restoring that horrible database—I couldn't very well abandon it, corrupted or no; it was critical infrastructure and people depended on it—and while hurriedly implementing workarounds for that malfunctioning climate control—one hundred and fifty-three levels of server racks could overheat catastrophically—I kept going over and over my prepared partnership speeches, trying to select the most effective one.

I had a Casual Approach: "Hey, I see there's a nice little co-working space available up on level one seventy-three." And I had a Professional Approach: "Sofia, I believe our skills complement each other perfectly. I think we could build something sustainable together. Will you consider a business partnership with me?" I even had a Straightforward Approach: "Sofia, I'm going to need a partner for this next venture, and I can't think of anyone I would rather work with than you."

Actually, though I wouldn't even have admitted this to Sofia, much less to anyone else, I loved her in more than a professional way. But even if we both had been interested in that kind of relationship (neither of us had ever expressed such interest) I knew that Sofia relished her independence too much to ever consider anything beyond a professional partnership.

So I rehearsed my various approaches, realizing that when the time came I would probably be so tongue-tied I'd be capable of no more than a blurted, "Will you partner with me?" and I struggled with authentication tokens and malfunctioning climate controls, and I managed somehow to leave my workstation at five minutes to ten.

Sofia worked down on the hundred fortieth level, thirteen levels away. It never took more than two or three minutes to get to her station, so I was giving myself plenty of time.

But then the network went down.

I tried to access the transit system, and nothing happened. I couldn't understand it.

The automated transit pods had always arrived before, within thirty seconds of being summoned. This was a local line, with pods that traveled between the hundred thirty-third level and the hundred sixty-seventh level, where it was possible to make connections for either the next local or for the express. So the nearest pod couldn't be more than twenty levels away. And this was a non-rush hour.

I tried again, and then I waited some more. I looked at my watch and it was three minutes to ten. Two minutes, and no pod! If it didn't arrive this instant, this second, I would be late.

It didn't arrive.

I vacillated, not knowing what to do next. Stay, hoping the pod would come after all? Or hurry back to my workstation and message Sofia, to give her advance warning that I would be late?

Ten more seconds, and still no pod. I chose the second alternative, raced back down the corridor, and authenticated my way into my workspace. I tried to message Sofia, and the screen lit up with red letters on black: COMMUNICATIONS OFFLINE.

Of course! The entire network was down. Sofia couldn't receive messages. And she knew what I wanted to say to her, so quite naturally she would be waiting, unable to understand why I hadn't arrived.

Frantic, I dashed from the workspace again, back down the corridor to the transit station, and pressed that blasted call button with all my weight. Even if a pod should arrive right now, I would still be almost a minute late.

No matter. It didn't arrive.

I would have been in a howling rage anyway, but this impossibility piled on top of all the other annoyances and breakdowns of the day was just too much. I went into a frenzy, and kicked the transit station wall three times before I realized I was hurting myself more than I was hurting the wall. I limped back to the workspace, fuming, slammed the door behind me, grabbed the facility directory and looked up the number of the Infrastructure Staff. I tried calling, prepared to register a complaint so loud they'd hear me in sub-basement three.

I got some more letters that spelled: NETWORK UNAVAILABLE.

It took three tries before I got through to a harried-looking female technician. "My name is Lucas!" I bellowed. "Lucas Ramirez! I work on the hundred and fifty-third level! I just tried to summon a transit pod and—"

"The-transit-system-is-offline." She said it very rapidly, as though she were growing very used to saying it.

It only stopped me for a second. "Offline? What do you mean offline? Transit systems don't just go offline!" I told her.

"We-will-resume-service-as-soon-as-possible," she rattled. My bellowing was bouncing off her like packets off a firewall.

I changed tactics. First I inhaled, making a production out of it, giving myself a chance to calm down a bit. And then I asked, as rationally as you could please, "Would you mind terribly telling me why the transit system is offline?"

"I-am-sorry-sir-but-that—"

"Stop," I said. I said it quietly, too, but she stopped. I saw her looking at me. She hadn't done that before, she'd merely gazed blankly at her screen and parroted her responses.

But now she was actually looking at me.

I took advantage of the fact. Calmly, rationally, I said to her, "I would like to tell you something, Miss. I would like to tell you just what you people have done to me by taking the transit system offline. You have ruined my life."

She blinked, open-mouthed. "Ruined your life?"

"Precisely." I found it necessary to inhale again, even more slowly than before. "I was on my way," I explained, "to propose a partnership to a woman whom I deeply respect and admire. In every way but one, she is the perfect partner. Do you understand me?"

She nodded, wide-eyed. I had stumbled on a romantic, though I was too preoccupied to notice it at the time.

"In every way but one," I continued. "She has one small quirk, a fixation about punctuality. And I was supposed to meet her at ten o'clock. I'm late!" I gestured emphatically at the screen. "Do you realize what you've done, taking the transit system offline? Not only won't she partner with me, she won't even speak to me! Not now! Not after this!"

"Sir," she said tremulously, "please don't shout."

"I'm not shouting!"

"Sir, I'm terribly sorry. I understand your—"

"You understand?" I trembled with speechless fury.

She looked all about her, and then leaned closer to the screen. "We're not supposed to give this information out, sir," she said, her voice low, "but I'm going to tell you, so you'll understand why we had to do it. I think it's perfectly awful that it had to ruin things for you this way. But the fact of the matter is—" she leaned even closer to the screen—"there's an intruder in the server room."

It was my turn to be stunned.

I just gaped at her. "A—a what?"

"An intruder. She was discovered on the hundred forty-seventh level, and managed to get into the main server room before Security could catch her. She locked it down from the inside. But Security is doing everything it can think of to get her out."

"Well—but why should there be any problem about getting her out?"

"She has administrative access. We can't control anything from outside at all. And when anyone tries to get into the server room, she threatens to wipe all the data."

That sounded catastrophic. "She threatens to wipe everything?"

"She has root access," the technician explained, "and she's holding the entire system hostage."

"Oh," I said. "So it might take a while."

She leaned so close this time that even I, distracted as I was, took note of her concerned expression. She whispered, "They're afraid they'll have to negotiate with her."

"Oh, no!"

She nodded solemnly. "I'm terribly sorry, sir," she said. Then she glanced to her right, suddenly straightened up again, and said, "We-will-resume-service-as-soon-as-possible." Click. Blank screen.

For a minute or two, all I could do was sit and absorb what I'd been told. An intruder in the server room! An intruder who had managed to work her way all the way up to the hundred forty-seventh level before being detected!

What in the world was the matter with Security? If things were getting that lax, the Facility was doomed, encryption or no. Who knew how many more intruders there were in the Facility, still undetected?

Until that moment, the state of isolation in which we all lived had had no reality for me. The Facility, after all, was self-sufficient and completely secure. No one ever left, no one ever entered. Within our walls, we were a community, two hundred levels high. The ever-present threat of other facilities had never been more for me—or for most other people either, I suspected—than occasional supply drones that didn't return, occasional intruders shot down as they tried to sneak into the building, occasional agents of our own leaving the Facility in tiny shielded vehicles, hoping to get safely within another facility and bring back intelligence of any immediate threats and dangers that facility might be planning for us. Most agents didn't return; most drones did. And within the Facility life was full, the knowledge of external dangers merely lurking at the backs of our minds. After all, those external dangers had been no more than potential for decades, since what Dr. Morrison called the Information Wars.

Dr. Morrison—Advanced Facility History, when I was fifteen years old—had private names for every major conflict of the twenty-first century. There was the First Cyber War, the Second Cyber War, and the Great Network Collapse, known to the textbooks of course as the Information Wars.

The rise of the Facilities, according to Dr. Morrison, was the result of many many factors, but two of the most important were the population concentration and the Geneva Protocols. The population concentration, of course, meant that there were continuously more and more people but never any more space. So that housing, in the historically short time of one century, made a complete transformation from horizontal expansion to vertical. Before 2000, the vast majority of human beings lived in structures of from one to five stories. By 2100, everybody lived in Facilities. From the very beginning, small attempts were made to make these Facilities more than dwelling places. By mid-century, Facilities already included restaurants, shopping centers, childcare services, maintenance hubs and a host of other adjuncts. By the end of the century, the Facilities were completely self-sufficient, with food grown hydroponically in the sub-basements, separate levels set aside for schools and medical centers and manufacturing, robot supply drones capable of seeking out raw materials unavailable within the Facilities themselves and so on. And all because of, among other things, the population concentration.

And the Geneva Protocols.

It seems there was a power-struggle between two sets of then-existing nations (they were something like Facilities, only horizontal instead of vertical) and both sets were equipped with cyber weapons. The Geneva Protocols began by stating that infrastructure warfare was unthinkable, and added that just in case anyone happened to think of it only tactical cyber weapons could be used. No strategic cyber weapons. (A tactical weapon is something you use on military systems, and a strategic weapon is something you use on civilian infrastructure.) Oddly enough, when somebody did think of the war, both sides adhered to the Geneva Protocols, which meant that no Facilities had their core systems destroyed.

Of course, they made up for this as best they could by using tactical cyber weapons all over the place. After the war almost the whole network infrastructure was quite dangerously compromised. Except for the Facilities. Or at least those of them which had in time installed the quantum encryption which had been invented on the very eve of battle, and which deflected intrusion attempts.

However, what with all of the other protocols which were broken during the Information Wars, by the time it was finished nobody was quite sure any more who was on whose side. That facility over there on the horizon might be an ally. And then again it might not. Since they weren't sure either, it was risky to expose yourself in order to ask.

And so life went on, with little to remind us of the dangers lurking Outside. The basic policy of Eternal Vigilance and Constant Monitoring was left to Security. The rest of us simply lived our lives and let it go at that.

But now there was an intruder in the server room.

When I thought of how deeply she had penetrated our defenses, and of how many others there might be, still penetrating, I shuddered. The walls were our safeguards only so long as all potential enemies were on the other side of them.

I sat shaken, digesting this news, until suddenly I remembered Sofia.

I leaped to my feet, reading from my watch that it was now ten-fifteen. I dashed once more from the workspace and down the corridor to the transit station, praying that the intruder had been captured by now and that Sofia would agree with me that an intruder in the server room was good and sufficient reason for me to be late.

The system was still down. At least, the transit pods were still unavailable.

I sagged against the wall, thinking dismal thoughts. Then I noticed the door to the right of the transit station. Through that door were the maintenance stairs.

I hadn't paid any attention to it before. No one ever uses the stairs except adventurous young technicians playing capture-the-flag, running up and down from landing to landing. I myself hadn't set foot on a flight of stairs since I was twelve years old.

Actually, the whole idea of stairs was ridiculous. We had transit pods, didn't we? Usually, I mean, when they didn't contain intruders or weren't offline due to security breaches. So what was the use of stairs?

Well, according to Dr. Morrison (a walking database of unnecessary information), the Facility had been built when there still had been such things as building codes, anachronistic even then, which required emergency stairs connecting all two hundred levels of the structure. The code mandated sixteen flights of stairs per level—eight ascending and eight descending from various access points spread across each floor. A tremendous redundancy, Dr. Morrison had called it, though he'd conceded it made evacuation calculations simpler.

Of course, Sofia had mentioned once that maintenance records showed some stairwells had been sealed during the Resource Conservation Initiative of 2087. "Six hundred flights blocked off with plasteel barriers," she'd told me, shaking her head at the inefficiency of the old building codes. "Twenty-six hundred active stairwells remaining. Still far more than anyone could ever need." She was always complaining about redundant systems—said they complicated her supply chain models unnecessarily.

And now, after all these years, the stairs might prove useful after all. It was only thirteen levels to Sofia's workspace. The main stairwell I was looking at had a single flight per level—one of the sixteen originally installed on each floor. Thirteen flights, sixteen steps per flight. That meant two hundred and eight steps.

Could I descend two hundred and eight steps for my potential business partner? I could. If the door would open.

It would, though reluctantly. Who knew how many years it had been since last this door had been opened? It squeaked and groaned and finally opened halfway. I stepped through to the dusty landing, took a deep breath, and started down. Eight steps and a landing, eight steps and a level. Eight steps and a landing, eight steps and a level.

On the landing between one fifty and one forty-nine, there was a small door. I paused, looking curiously at it, and saw that at one time letters had been stenciled on it. The letters had long since faded, but they left a lighter residue of dust than that which covered the rest of the door. And so the words could still be read, if with difficulty.

I read them. They said:

EMERGENCY ACCESS
SERVER ROOM
AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL
ONLY
KEEP LOCKED

I frowned, wondering immediately why this door wasn't being firmly guarded by at least a squad of Security personnel. Half a dozen possible answers flashed through my mind. The more recent maps might simply have omitted this discarded and unnecessary door. It might be sealed shut on the other side—one of those six hundred blocked-off stairwell access points, perhaps. Security might have caught the intruder already. Somebody in authority might simply have made an error in judgment.

As I stood there, pondering these possibilities, the door opened and the intruder came out, holding a device that looked like it could cause serious harm.

She couldn't have been anyone else but the intruder. The device, in the first place. The fact that she looked harried and upset and terribly nervous, in the second place. And, of course, the fact that she came from the server room.

Looking back, I think she must have been just as startled as I when we came face to face like that. We formed a brief tableau, both of us open-mouthed and wide-eyed.

Unfortunately, she recovered first.

She closed the emergency door behind her, quickly but quietly. Her device stopped waving around and instead pointed directly at my middle. "Don't move!" she whispered harshly. "Don't make a sound!"

I did exactly as I was told. I didn't move and I didn't make a sound. Which left me quite free to study her.

She was rather tall, perhaps three inches taller than me, with sharp features and intense eyes. She wore dark clothing, practical for moving unseen. She looked exactly like an intruder... which is to say that she didn't look like an intruder, she looked remarkably ordinary.

Her gaze darted this way and that. Then she gestured with her free hand at the descending stairs and whispered, "Where do they go?"

I had to clear my throat before I could speak. "All the way down," I said.

"Good," she said—just as we both heard a sudden raucous squealing from perhaps four flights down, a squealing which could be nothing but the opening of a corridor door. It was followed by the heavy thud of ascending boots. Security!

But if I had any visions of imminent rescue, the intruder dashed them. She said, "Where do you work?"

"One fifty-three," I said. This was a desperate and dangerous woman. I knew my only slim chance of safety lay in answering her questions promptly, cooperating with her until and unless I saw a chance to either escape or capture her.

"All right," she whispered. "Go on." She prodded me with the device.

And so we went back up the stairs to one fifty-three, and stopped at the door. She stood close behind me, the device pressed against my back, and grated in my ear, "I'll have this device in my pocket. If you make one false move I'll use it. Now, we're going to your workspace. We're colleagues, just walking along together. You got that?"

I nodded.

"All right. Let's go."

We went. I have never in my life seen that long corridor quite so empty as it was right then. No one came out of any of the workspaces, no one emerged from any of the branch corridors. We walked to my workspace. I authenticated the door and we went inside.

Once the door was closed behind us, she visibly relaxed, sagging against the door, her device hand hanging limp at her side, a nervous smile playing across her lips.

I looked at her, judging the distance between us, wondering if I could leap at her before she could bring the device up again. But she must have read my intentions on my face. She straightened, shaking her head. She said, "Don't try it. I don't want to hurt you. I don't want to hurt anybody, but I will if I have to. We'll just wait here together until the search passes us. Then I'll secure you, so you won't be able to alert Security too soon, and I'll leave. If you don't try any silly heroics, nothing will happen to you."

"You'll never get away," I told her. "The whole Facility is on alert."

"You let me worry about that," she said. She licked her lips. "You got any coffee?"

"Yes."

"Make me a cup. And don't get any bright ideas about using it as a weapon."

"I only have my day's allotment," I protested. "Just enough for two cups, morning and afternoon."

"Two cups is fine," she said. "One for each of us."

And now I had yet another grudge against this blasted intruder. Which reminded me again of Sofia. From the looks of things, I wasn't ever going to get to her workspace. By now she was probably mourning our potential partnership and might even have Security searching for my remains.

As I made the coffee, she asked me questions. My name first, and then, "What do you do for a living?"

I thought fast. "I'm a supply chain analyst," I said. That was a lie, of course, but I'd heard enough about supply chain management from Sofia to be able to maintain the fiction should she question me further about it.

Actually, I was a cybersecurity specialist. The subjects I worked on included intrusion detection, threat analysis and penetration testing—talents I would prefer to disclose to her in my own fashion, when the time came.

She was quiet for a moment. "What about the supply drones? Do you ever analyze their data logs?"

I had no idea what she was talking about, and admitted as much.

"When they come back," she said. "What kind of data do they collect about conditions outside? Don't you people ever review them?"

"Of course not," I told her. I was on secure ground now, with Sofia's information to guide me. "All data is sanitized and verified before it's integrated into our systems."

"I know that," she said impatiently. "But don't you ever analyze the raw data before sanitizing it?"

"No. Why should we?"

"To find out what conditions are actually like outside."

"For what? Who cares about that?"

She frowned bitterly. "The same answer," she muttered, more to herself than to me. "The same answer every time. You people have locked yourselves in your towers and you're ready to stay in them forever."

I looked around at my workspace. "Rather a well-equipped tower," I told her.

"But a tower nevertheless." She leaned toward me, her eyes gleaming with intensity. "Don't you ever wish to go Outside?"

Incredible! I nearly spilled boiling coffee all over myself. "Outside? Of course not!"

"The same thing," she grumbled, "over and over again. Always the same response. Listen, you! Do you realize how long it took humanity to build these networks? The long slow painful development of technology, for centuries, before we ever made that first step toward global connection?"

"I have no idea," I told her.

"I'll tell you this," she said forcefully. "A lot longer than it took for us to disconnect and isolate ourselves again." She started pacing the floor, waving the device around in an agitated fashion as she talked. "Is this the natural state of humanity? It is not. Is this even a desirable state for humanity? It is definitely not." She spun back to face me, pointing the device at me again, but this time she pointed it as though it were a finger, not a weapon. "Listen, you," she snapped. "Humanity was progressing. For all our mistakes and excesses, we were growing. Our dreams were getting bigger and better all the time. We were planning to tackle space! The moon first, and then the planets, and finally the stars. The whole universe was out there, waiting to be explored. And humanity was reaching out for it." She glared as though daring me to doubt it.

I decided that this woman was doubly dangerous. Not only was she an intruder, she was also unstable. So I had two reasons for humoring her. I nodded politely.

"So what happened?" she demanded, and immediately answered herself. "I'll tell you what happened! Just as we were about to make that first giant leap, humanity got scared. That's all it was, just a crisis of confidence. So what did humanity do? I'll tell you what we did. We turned around and we ran all the way back to isolated communities, our collective tail between our legs. That's what we did!"

To say that all of this was incomprehensible would be an extreme understatement. I fulfilled my obligation to this insane dialogue by saying, "Here's your coffee."

"Put it on the desk," she said, switching instantly from raving idealist to watchful intruder.

I put it on the desk. She drank deep, then carried the cup across the room and sat down in my chair. She studied me narrowly, and suddenly said, "What did they tell you I was? A spy?"

"An intruder," I said.

She grinned bitterly. "Of course. The fools! Intruder! What do you suppose I'm going to steal?"

She asked the question so violently and urgently that I knew I had to answer quickly and well, or the unstable side would return. "I—I wouldn't know, exactly," I stammered. "Data, I suppose. Intelligence."

"Intelligence? What intelligence? Your facility operates on the same principles as every other facility. There's nothing unique here."

"The security protocols—" I started.

"The security protocols," she interrupted me, "are standard. If you mean the quantum encryption, it's the same system everyone uses."

"If you say so," I replied stiffly. Security claimed that we had superior protection. I chose to believe Security over an enemy intruder.

"Your facility sends out agents, too, doesn't it?" she demanded.

"Well, of course."

"And what are they supposed to do?"

"Well—" It was such a pointless question, it seemed silly to even answer it. "They're supposed to look for indications of an attack by one of the other facilities."

"And do they find any indications, ever?"

"I'm sure I don't know," I told her coldly. "That would be classified information."

"You bet it would," she said, with malicious satisfaction. "All right, if that's what your agents are doing, and if I'm an intruder, then it follows that I'm doing the same thing, right?"

"I don't follow you," I admitted.

"If I'm an intruder," she said impatiently, "then I'm supposed to look for indications of an attack by you people on my Facility."

I shrugged. "If that's your mission," I said, "then that's your mission."

She got suddenly red-faced, and jumped to her feet. "That's not my mission, you stubborn fool!" she shouted. "I'm not an intruder! If I were an intruder, then that would be my mission!"

The unstable side had returned, in full force. "All right," I said hastily. "All right, whatever you say."

She glowered at me a moment longer, then shouted, "Bah!" and dropped back into the chair.

She breathed rather heavily for a while, glaring at the floor, then looked at me again. "All right, listen. What if I were to tell you that I had found evidence that you people were planning to attack my Facility?"

I stared at her. "That's impossible!" I cried. "We aren't planning to attack anybody! We just want to be left alone!"

"How do I know that?" she demanded.

"It's the truth! What would we want to attack anybody for?"

"Ah hah!" She sat forward, tensed, pointing the device at me like a finger again. "Now, then," she said. "If you know it doesn't make any sense for this Facility to attack any other facility, then why in the world should you think they might see some advantage in attacking you?"

I shook my head, dumbfounded. "I can't answer a question like that," I said. "How do I know what they're thinking?"

"They're human beings, aren't they?" she cried. "Like you? Like me? Like all the other people in this fortress?"

"Now, wait a minute—"

"No!" she shouted. "You wait a minute! I want to tell you something. You think I'm an intruder. That incompetent Security force thinks I'm an intruder. That administrator who reported me thinks I'm an intruder. But I'm not an intruder, and I'm going to tell you what I am."

I waited, looking as attentive as possible.

"I come," she said, "from a Facility about eighty miles north of here. I came here on foot, without any sort of protective equipment at all."

The unstable side was back. I didn't say a word. I didn't want to set off the violence that was so obviously in this person.

"The environmental conditions," she went on, "are safe. They're practically as good as they were before the Information Wars. I don't know how long they've been that good, but I would guess about ten years, at the very least." She leaned forward again, urgent and serious. "The world is safe out there now. Humanity can come back out of the fortresses again. We can start building the dreams again. And this time we can build better, because we have the horrible example of the recent past to guide us away from the pitfalls. There's no need any longer for the Facilities."

And that was like saying there's no need any longer for shelter, but I didn't say so. I didn't say anything at all.

"I'm a trained environmental scientist," she went on. "In my facility, I worked on air quality monitoring. Theoretically, I believed that there was a chance the environment Outside was recovering by now, though we had no idea exactly how much damage had been done by the wars. But I wanted to test the theory through field research, and the Council wouldn't let me. They claimed public safety, but I knew better. If the Outside were safe and the Facilities were no longer needed, then the Council was out of power, and they knew it.

"So I left. I walked out. And I've been traveling from Facility to Facility, trying to spread the word. Trying to get people to understand that isolation isn't necessary anymore. That we can rebuild a connected world. That the principles of sustainable business and ethical decision-making can guide us to something better than what we had before."

She paused, looking at me intently. "Do you understand what I'm saying? This isn't about espionage or warfare. This is about freedom. About choice. About remembering that we're all part of the same species, the same world."

I stared at her, my mind reeling. Everything she was saying contradicted everything I'd been taught, everything I believed. And yet...

"You're insane," I said quietly.

She smiled sadly. "Maybe. Or maybe everyone else is. That's the question, isn't it? Who decides what's rational? The people who benefit from the current system? Or the people who dare to question it?"

Before I could respond, we both heard a sound outside my door. Heavy footsteps. Multiple people.

Security had found us.

The woman—I couldn't think of her as just an intruder anymore—looked at me one last time. "Think about what I said. Please. For your own sake, and for everyone's."

Then she moved with surprising speed, securing me to my chair with some kind of quick-release restraint, and disappeared through a maintenance hatch I hadn't even known existed in my own workspace.

By the time Security broke through my door, she was gone.

And I was left with questions I couldn't answer, and doubts I couldn't shake.

Had we really imprisoned ourselves? Were we maintaining a siege mentality long after the actual threat had passed? Was our isolation a necessary protection, or a comfortable prison?

I didn't know. But for the first time in my life, I wanted to find out.

And I never did make it to Sofia's workspace that day. Though when I finally did see her, two days later, and explained everything that had happened, she surprised me.

"You know," she said thoughtfully, "I've always wondered why the supply drones never bring back any environmental data. It's like we don't want to know."

"Yeah," I said. "It's exactly like that."

I mentioned the stairwell, how it had been an unexpected lifeline during the crisis. Sofia nodded knowingly. "All those redundant systems," she said. "The building codes required sixteen flights per level when this place was built—can you imagine? Across all two hundred levels. Most facilities our size have sealed off at least a quarter of them by now."

"A quarter seems like a lot," I said, thinking of that dark, dusty stairwell.

"Ours sealed off six hundred during the Resource Conservation Initiative," she replied. "Standard procedure. The maintenance costs weren't justified when no one uses them anyway."

We looked at each other, and I saw the same questions in her eyes that were in mine.
